To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a compiler method that allocates objects to scratch-pad memory for embedded systems whose scratch-pad memory sizes are unknown at compile-time.

we have developed a memory allocation scheme for scratch-pad memory whose allocation decisions are based on a compile-time-unknow SPM size, that our allocation scheme is portable, that it is fast, and that it has low overhead.
our method is portable to any SPM size, and that it achieves an average 36% speedup versus an all-DRAM allocation, while having only 1% run-time overhead.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of data allocation in embedded systems with SPM.
the design of an embedded memory allocator that can be used in a wide range of embedded processors with different scratch-pad memory size and different memory hierarchy.
the following questions: 1) How can a compiler generate an executable that uses a scratch-pad memory (a fast, on-chip SRAM) without knowing the size of the scratch-pad memory at compile-time?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our scheme is the first to achieve a good balance between the benefits of SPM and the portability of the executable.
the proposed approach is the first to enable the use of SPM in a wide range of embedded systems.
our method is the first to achieve the benefits of scratch-pad memory for systems whose SPM size is unknown at the time of code compilation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our scheme provides the best of both worlds: the speedup and real-time predictability of SPM and the portability of DRAM.

we have shown how to use SPM for programs whose size is not known at compile-time and that we have shown that the resulting performance is close to the performance achievable with an optimal static allocation.
our scheme is the only one that allows for a post-compiler allocation to SPM and is the first that is portable across SPCs of different sizes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SPMs can be effectively used in systems that use downloaded code, even though the SPM sizes are unknown at compile-time.

a compiler-managed scratch-pad memory is a viable alternative to cache in embedded systems, even when the SPM size is unknown at run-time, and thus even when the SPCM is not a permanent part of the system.
the SPM allocation problem is not just an academic exercise but is a practical problem for embedded systems.
